summary: State f70a73a9ba0dcaa7 (source level, no machine-IR edits) is 3.88x faster than amdclang's build: 56.3 us vs 218.6 us at 240 pairs, CI 3.8715 to 3.8875; static check passes (4 undefined_read warnings, checked by hand to be false positives), battery 77/77. Reference headroom is 10.8, so the baseline is not memory bound: it is bound by serial load rounds and LDS reduction trees in one wave per query (per 64-key tile: 4 K-load rounds, 8 V-load rounds, 2 six-level LDS reductions with 17 barriers). The winning state launches grid cdiv(NQ,4) x block 256: one workgroup computes 4 queries, so each K row and V row is loaded once and reused for 4 queries; it works in two passes per supertile of up to 2048 keys (pass A: all scores, 16 x4 K loads in flight per thread, q as SGPR operands, scores kept in LDS; one max reduction per query per supertile instead of one per tile; pass B: p = exp2((s - m) * log2 e), V read as x4 loads by 16 key groups x 16 column groups, partial sums combined across threads once at the end). Results meet the manifest tolerance but are not bit-identical (different summation order, exp2 builtin instead of expf for p, max taken per supertile). Caveat: the path with more than one supertile (NK > 2048) is not known to be exercised by the battery on this binary; a sibling build of the same source with NT=64, ST=64 (ee171df353f24377) passes the battery 77/77 with 3 supertiles at NK=150, which tests the logic but not this binary at that size. Levers left untried for lack of budget: machine-IR edits on the best state (K loads of the next tile in flight during the q loop using VGPRs above 128; V loads issued before the p computation), block 512, coarsen / unroll_loads on the best state.

friction: static_check undefined_read is path-insensitive: in every multi-query state (67e9c646840792ec .Lft13/.Lft16/.Lft19/.Lft22 `ds_read_b128 v[8:11], v92 offset:34848`; f70a73a9ba0dcaa7 the same on v1) the register is written in both arms of an entry branch whose outcome is replayed by a second branch on a saved condition (s[0:1] = 0 / -1 then s_andn2_b64 vcc, exec, s[0:1]). I had to read the listing to confirm each one is a false positive; a warning that named the path it believes is undefined would have made that a one-line check.

State listings above about 1000 instructions exceed the tool-result limit (state() on 635b35, d56626, fcb1c5, f70a73 returned 'exceeds maximum allowed tokens' and was dumped to a file with the listing as one JSON string line). I could only inspect them with regex -o greps. A `state(ref, block=...)` / line-range option, or a grep over the listing (e.g. all writes of a register, all scratch ops with their block), is needed for source-level states of this size.

check() reports vgpr_spills / scratch_bytes only after the GPU battery; features() does not report them. Three states (635b35, 1d1ef5, d56626/fcb1c5) were only recognisable as spill-bound from the vmem count. Spill counts per loop in features() (or in the source() result) would have saved two timed candidates.

56002ed43a5db158: static_check rejects amdclang's own SGPR spill code (`v_readlane_b32 vcc_lo, v123, 20`: 'a vcc_lo register is not allowed here (OPR_SREG_NOVCC)'). Either accept it or report 'the compiler spilled N SGPRs' as one finding.

amdclang's choices that had to be defeated by trial and error at the source level, each costing a compile: it hoists wave-uniform q loads into SGPRs until it spills them; its loop vectorizer packs a 4-iteration query loop into v_pk_fma pairs and duplicates the K registers; it stays within 128 VGPRs and spills beyond. No way from source() to pass flags (e.g. disable SLP/loop vectorization, raise the VGPR limit).

No way to run the battery on a chosen shape: the winning state has a path (more than one 2048-key supertile, NK > 2048) that I could not show to be exercised; `info()` gives the base shape NK=150 and the variants are hidden. I had to build a sibling state with a 64-key supertile to test the logic. A `check(ref, shapes={...})` or a list of the battery's shape variants would close this.

No per-phase timing or diagnostic bench of an incomplete kernel: whether the remaining 36 us is the q scalar-load rounds, the K/V load rounds, LDS, or barrier waits between the 4 waves had to be inferred from full variants (R = 2/4/8, block 64/256/1024).

bench at 60 pairs returned outcome 'win' with speedup 2.21 and CI 1.91-2.73 for 67e9c646840792ec while reference_ms was 0.324 instead of 0.220: a disturbed run is only visible by comparing reference_ms with earlier runs. A flag when reference_ms deviates from the session's reference timing, or an automatic rerun, would prevent a wrong number being recorded.

traffic / headroom assume each tensor element is read once; this kernel reads K and V once per workgroup (512 times here), so tb_per_s (0.04) is off by orders of magnitude and the kernel's headroom figure is not meaningful.
lessons: fa_attention (reference headroom 10.8, not memory bound): the baseline is one 64-thread wave per query that runs, per 64-key tile, 4 K-load rounds, 8 V-load rounds and two 6-level LDS reductions (17 barriers). Removing the per-tile reductions (two passes: all scores to LDS, one max per 2048 keys, then p and V) and batching loads (16 x4 K loads per wait, V as 16 x4 loads) gave only 1.45x with one query per wave (151.7 us).

Sharing loads across queries is what paid: 4 queries per workgroup, each K row and V row loaded once and used 4 times, with q as SGPR operands from s_load_dwordx16: 1.94x at block 64 (113.4 us), 3.88x at block 256 (56.3 us). The count has an optimum: at block 256, 2 queries 2.52x (86.9 us), 4 queries 3.88x, 8 queries 3.00x (73.1 us; the 8-query build also needed V loads in quarters). Both bytes loaded and serial rounds per wave count.
More waves per workgroup shorten each wave's serial chain: block 64 -> 256 with the same source went from 113.4 us to 56.3 us; block 1024 was slower again (67.8 us).
Barriers in a one-wave workgroup are nearly free: deleting the 2 per-tile s_barrier (64 per wave) measured 1.008 (CI 1.0056-1.0106), parity.

Scratch spills are fatal in a loop: the 4-query and 2-query builds with 203 and 115 spill instructions both ran at 0.72x of the baseline (about 305 us), while the spill-free 4-query build ran at 1.94x. Check `vgpr_spills` in check() resources (or scratch_* in the listing) before timing a source state.

Source-level controls that were needed with this amdclang: `#pragma clang loop unroll(disable) vectorize(disable) interleave(disable)` on a short loop over queries (otherwise it is vectorized into v_pk_fma pairs with duplicated operand registers); keeping that loop un-unrolled so q loads are not hoisted into more SGPRs than exist; __builtin_fmaf for the dot product; per-query accumulators as unrolled scalars; loads split into a non-unrolled inner loop (8 x4 loads per step) to stay under 128 VGPRs.

Linear accumulators can be kept partial per thread and combined once at the end: o = o * rescale + acc and l are linear, so 16 key groups x 16 column groups each hold a float4 partial and one LDS pass at the end sums them; this turns 64 strided dword loads per thread per tile into 16 x4 loads without any per-tile cross-thread combine.

A 60-pair bench can be badly wrong when the device is disturbed: one run gave 2.21 (CI 1.91-2.73) with reference_ms 0.324 where the repeat at 240 pairs gave 1.937 (CI 1.934-1.939) with reference_ms 0.220. Compare reference_ms with the known baseline before believing a number.

session.final:
Shipped state `f70a73a9ba0dcaa7`: **3.88x** over amdclang (56.3 us vs 218.6 us at 240 pairs, CI 3.87–3.89). It passes the static check and the full battery (77/77), and the report is recorded.

**Which case this is:** reference headroom is 10.8, so the baseline is not memory bound. It was bound by serial load rounds and shared-memory reduction trees in a single wave per query.

**What the winning state does differently (source level only):**
- **Launch:** grid `cdiv(NQ, 4)` with 256-thread blocks instead of `NQ` with 64.
- **Shared loads:** one workgroup computes 4 queries, so each K row and V row is loaded once and reused four times.
- **Two passes per 2048 keys:** first all scores (kept in shared memory, one max reduction per query), then the exponentials and the V accumulation. The baseline did two reduction trees per 64-key tile.
- **Wide V loads:** threads hold partial sums over 16 key groups × 16 column groups and combine them once at the end.

Results meet the manifest tolerance but are not bit-identical to the baseline (different summation order, `exp2` builtin for the probabilities).

| Variant | State | Speedup |
|---|---|---|
| 1 query per wave, block 64 | `a2100732` | 1.45x |
| 4 queries, block 64 | `67e9c646` | 1.94x |
| 2 queries, block 256 | `45abb436` | 2.52x |
| 8 queries, block 256 | `ddc18f67` | 3.00x |
| 4 queries, block 1024 | `22ef79ac` | 3.24x |
| **4 queries, block 256** | `f70a73a9` | **3.88x** |

Things to know before relying on it:
- **Untested path on this binary:** inputs with more than 2048 keys take a second pass through the outer loop, and I could not confirm the battery exercises that. A sibling build of the same source with a 64-key outer block (`ee171df3`) passes 77/77 with three such passes, which tests the logic but not this binary at that size.
- **Static-check warnings:** the shipped state carries 4 `undefined_read` warnings. I read the listing and they are false positives: the register is written on both arms of the entry bran
